title: India's First Bullet Train Revealed: 280 Kmph Test Speed, 557 Passengers, Eight Coaches
excerpt: The BEML-built B28 for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor is rated at 280 kmph in testing and 249 kmph in planned service, with seven standard-class coaches, one executive coach, Wi-Fi infotainment and level boarding.
body:
• India's first indigenous bullet train, the B28, is being built by BEML in Bengaluru for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail corridor, according to the Ministry of Railways.
  • Its maximum test speed is 280 kmph; its planned operational speed is 249 kmph — the two figures describe testing and passenger service respectively, and are not interchangeable.
  • The eight-coach train is about 202 metres long and carries 557 passengers: seven standard-class coaches with 3x2 seating and one executive-class coach with 2x2 seating, including two spaces for passengers with reduced mobility.
  • Features include Wi-Fi-based infotainment, information displays in English, Hindi and regional languages, bio-digester toilets, level boarding and wheelchair-friendly doors.

India's first indigenous bullet train is taking shape at Bharat Earth Movers Limited's (BEML) facility in Bengaluru, built for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail (MAHSR) corridor. The Ministry of Railways has set out the train's specifications: it is designed for Indian conditions, with passenger convenience, accessibility and operational efficiency at the forefront, and it marks a step toward domestic manufacturing capability in high-speed rail.

The Two Speeds, Stated Precisely

The headline figures need one distinction kept straight. The train's maximum test speed is 280 kmph — the speed it is designed to reach in testing. Its planned operational speed is 249 kmph — the speed planned for passenger service. Reports that quote only 280 kmph are quoting the test figure, not the speed at which passengers will travel.

Inside the Eight Coaches

The train, designated B28 in the feature reporting, is approximately 202 metres long and formed of eight coaches: four motor cars and four trailer cars. Seven coaches are standard class with 3x2 seating; one is executive class with 2x2 seating. Total capacity is 557 passengers, including two designated spaces for Divyangjan and Persons with Reduced Mobility. Two eight-coach trainsets can be coupled into a 16-coach formation for future operations. Driver's cabs at both ends carry an intelligent onboard control system intended to support decision-making and coordination with the operation control centre.

Inside, the coaches have ergonomically designed seats developed with Indian anthropometric requirements in mind, LED lighting, overhead baggage racks plus floor-mounted luggage stands for larger bags, and power outlets for laptops and mobile devices. Wide windows are fitted at every seating row. Toilets are bio-digester units designed to minimise effluent. Each coach has two heating, ventilation and air-conditioning units to regulate temperature and humidity.

Information, Accessibility and the Engineering Underneath

A Wi-Fi-based infotainment system offers preloaded entertainment content, and LCD displays provide passenger information in English, Hindi and regional languages, with public-address announcements and emergency talk-back units in the cabins and vestibules. Accessibility is built into the structure rather than added on: the coach floor aligns with platform height for level boarding, retractable footsteps reduce the gap at the doors, and there are wheelchair-friendly doors, dedicated seating and toilet facilities for passengers with reduced mobility, and Braille-enabled signage.

The train runs on a 25 kV, 50 Hz single-phase AC traction system, and its regenerative braking recovers energy during braking and feeds it back into the electrical system. The aerodynamic profile was developed using Computational Fluid Dynamics simulations, shaping the nose and carbody to reduce air resistance and turbulence and to mitigate tunnel pressure waves. Sound insulation, noise-damping coatings and aerodynamic fairings are intended to keep the cabin quiet at speed.

What Is Still Ahead

Jagran Josh's reporting on the revealed features puts the B28's launch in August 2027 and reports fares slated to start at a minimum of Rs 250 for short distances and reach approximately Rs 3,000 for the full Mumbai-Ahmedabad journey; those fare figures are reported plans, not a published tariff. What the Ministry's specifications establish now is the train itself — its formation, capacity, speeds and equipment — being manufactured in Bengaluru for a corridor that will be the diaspora's most visible test of whether India can build, not just buy, high-speed rail.
